message.content:
The total number of distinct positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large—on the order of **10⁴³** (roughly 100 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000).  

This figure, often called the *Shannon number*, comes from Claude Shannon’s 1950 estimate of the game‑tree complexity of chess. It represents an upper bound on the number of legal positions that can occur during a game, taking into account all the rules (piece placement, castling rights, en‑passant possibilities, etc.).  

For comparison:

| Quantity | Rough Estimate |
|----------|----------------|
| Legal positions | ~10⁴³ |
| Possible games (full move sequences) | ~10¹²⁰ |
| Possible arrangements of pieces on a board (ignoring rules) | 64! ≈ 10⁹⁴ |

So, while the exact count is still a subject of research and depends on how you define “legal” positions, the consensus is that there are on the order of 10⁴³ distinct arrangements that can arise in a chess game.
